extracted.intended_audience: journalism students and reporters learning to write accident/fire news stories
extracted.subtask_description: Writing news reports of fires, collisions, shipwrecks, mine explosions and other accidents: assembling facts (who/what/when/where), rescue and investigation details, human-interest elements, and technical/contextual data into clear leads and narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Victim identification
rubrics_metrics.description: List the names, ages, hometowns/residence, and nature of injuries (or death) of persons affected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show runs of names with ages and brief injury descriptions (e.g., 'Max Donelson, 42 years old, New York, bruised about body'). Use concise items for multiple victims so readers can see who was hurt or killed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause and investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Report any discovered or suspected cause of the accident and note official investigations into the cause (police, company officials, inspectors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece reports 'the police, on investigation, found a broken rail... agreed that this was the cause' and repeatedly notes that 'officials of the road are investigating'—give factual findings and indicate ongoing inquiries or unexplained elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official actions and legal follow-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Record arrests, charges, remands, inquests, and official determinations (e.g., arrests followed by discharge or remand to coroner).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text mentions 'Towerman Williamson ... was at once discharged' and 'Supt. Kivlin was arrested ... remand him to the coroner.' Include legal/procedural status and any court/inquest steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timetable and travel context
rubrics_metrics.description: Give departure/arrival times, schedules, the nature of the service (commuter train, express, passenger/sleeper), and passenger purpose or destination when relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The train left Philadelphia at 7:58 Saturday morning' and crowds bound for 'Princeton-Dartmouth'—these situate the event and explain who was aboard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rescue and emergency-response details
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe rescue operations, difficulty of extrication, dispatching of wrecking/relief trains or ambulances, and which agencies responded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passages detail reserves, ambulances, wrecking trains, and 'extricating the injured, which was a difficult task'—report timelines, resources sent, and on-scene challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property and valuables at risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Note valuable cargo or property affected (e.g., specie, mail car contents) and security measures taken at the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'In the mail car ... was more than $1,000,000 in specie ... A special guard was hurriedly placed around this car.' Mention such facts because they affect response and public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical/equipment details affecting outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe construction, materials, and equipment that influenced survivability or damage (e.g., steel cars, concrete flooring, lifeboat behavior, ship dimensions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text credits steel-car construction for preventing greater loss: 'They were of steel, with steel beams and concrete flooring ... there was no splintering of wood.' For ships, give tonnage, dimensions, and cargo as in the Alma E. A. Holmes entry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-interest and scene detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Include vivid human details about victims, survivors, or bystanders (state of dress, actions immediately after the event, crowd confusion, emotional reaction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: passengers 'half clad, into snow banks'; 'many left the hospitals and resumed their journey without giving their names.' Such details provide immediacy and color.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biographical context for notable victims
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide background on prominent individuals involved (positions held, previous achievements, affiliations) when a notable person is killed or injured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Spencer Trask piece gives career highlights, club memberships, and philanthropic ties—use biographical context to explain public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative arrangement and lead emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that the same facts can be arranged differently by different papers; compare versions to see differences in lead choice, emphasis, and narrative order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book explicitly states 'The following two stories should be compared' and 'illustrate different arrangements of the same material'—use comparisons to teach lead selection and organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of lead and narrative framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Select a lead that frames the angle (human drama, cause, death of a notable, rescue) and arrange subsequent material to support that lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One version leads with dramatic achievement-then-tragedy, another with concise facts. The instructor examples show how lead choice changes tone and reader focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution of speculative causes
rubrics_metrics.description: When assigning blame or cause reported as hearsay ('is said to have caused'), attribute properly and avoid presenting speculation as fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Failure of a brakeman ... is said to have caused the smashup.' Use qualifying phrases and attribute claims to sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of quotations to convey voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate direct speech from rescuers, officials, or witnesses to convey personality, urgency, or official positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotations such as 'The man who goes down after those men takes his life in his hand...' add immediacy and human voice—use them selectively to illuminate the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weather and environmental conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Report relevant weather, visibility, temperature, and sea/state of tide as factors contributing to the accident or rescue difficulty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: fog at Graves Light, 'temperature far below the freezing point' affecting partially dressed victims, and gale descriptions—these contextualize causation and survivability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical vessel/mining specifications and cargo
rubrics_metrics.description: Give ship/schooner dimensions, tonnage, cargo, and mine shaft data when pertinent to understanding the accident and its consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Alma Holmes entry lists gross/net tonnage, length, beam, depth and cargo (1819 tons of coal). Marianna mine descriptions include shaft numbers and ventilation/fanhouse status—these details matter to specialist readers and investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survivor/witness testimony and timeline
rubrics_metrics.description: Include first-person survivor accounts and construct a clear timeline of events from those accounts when available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leggett survivor Farrell's account supplies sequence (orders, lifeboat launches, capsizing) that clarifies what happened—use such testimony to build chronological narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety equipment status and paradoxes
rubrics_metrics.description: Report on safety measures present or absent and note anomalies where equipment meant to prevent disaster failed or impeded rescue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Marianna mine is described as 'the model mine of the world' yet was destroyed; 'the very machinery ... hampered the rescuers.' Point out such ironies for analysis and public accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community and social impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe crowds, mourning, public reaction, and effects on families and communities (panic, pleas, fundraising, mental breakdowns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accounts show 'five thousand women and children' at the mine, women becoming 'violently insane,' and subscriptions raised for rescue workers—these convey the wider human consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear chronological sequencing and organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure the story so that the sequence of events is clear — what happened first, what followed, rescue attempts, and subsequent investigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Across examples the narrative follows a chronological arc from incident to rescue to investigation; maintain clarity so readers can follow cause/effect and response.
